title: Ksitigarbha
hookLine: the bodhisattva who vows to help those in the lowest realms

lines: A DAUGHTER AFRAID FOR HER MOTHER.
A VISION OF A DARK SEA.
cards: A young woman's mother has died, and the daughter is afraid for her. Her mother, the story says, scorned the teaching and did harm in her life.
So the daughter sells the family house, brings offerings to a temple, and weeps before an image of a Buddha. A voice tells her to go home, sit, and call on that Buddha's name.
In a vision she's taken to the edge of a dark sea where beings suffer, and learns her mother has already been freed. Relief. And then she thinks of all those still in that sea.

teach.b: First, the vow. Back from the vision, before that Buddha's image, the daughter vows that through lifetimes to come she will help every being who suffers in the lowest realms.
The Sutra of the Past Vows of Ksitigarbha says that, after many lives, she became the bodhisattva Ksitigarbha.
A saying long linked to him puts the vow in one sharp line: not until the hells are empty will I become a Buddha. Second, the look.

teach.h: A PLAIN MONK WITH A STAFF AND A JEWEL.
teach.b: Where other bodhisattvas often wear crowns and jewels, in East Asia Ksitigarbha usually appears as a plain monk, head shaved, holding a staff hung with rings and a jewel that lights up the dark.
Dressed for walking into hard places, not for a throne.
Third, the name, usually given in English as earth store, or earth womb: the ground that holds treasure and holds seeds. The ground everyone stands on, the place no one looks at.
Fourth, the roadside. In China he is Dizang; in Japan, Jizo, whose small stone figures stand by roads, on mountain paths and in temple yards, sometimes dressed in red bibs and knitted caps.

teach.h: NOT UNTIL THE HELLS ARE EMPTY.
teach.b: Jizo is seen as a protector of travelers and of children, and families grieving a child, before birth or after, sometimes come to him with their grief. He goes to the low places, and stays.
If grief is heavy for you today, you don't have to carry it alone: in the US you can call or text 988, or reach local emergency help.

how: In East Asia, Buddhists turn to Ksitigarbha when someone has died, and the sutra of his vows is recited for the dead; in Japan, Jizo statues by roads and in temple yards are dressed and tended by local people.

o: the bodhisattva who vows to help beings in the lowest realms
a monk's staff hung with rings, carried on pilgrimage
a stone guardian that keeps evil spirits out of a home

games.q: the earth store: tap the pairs.
p: sold the house to make offerings

s: in East Asia, Ksitigarbha is usually shown in a crown and fine jewels
he usually appears as a plain monk, with a staff and a jewel that lights the dark.
in the sutra, a daughter's grief for her mother leads to the vow
after her mother is freed, she vows to help all who suffer in the lowest realms.
in Japan, Jizo watches only over the dead
he is seen as a protector of travelers and of children too.

games.q: your mother has died, and you were afraid for her. in a vision you learn she has been freed. then you think of all the others still suffering in that dark sea. what do you do?
o: go home relieved, the matter settled
vow to help every being still suffering there
ask that only your own family be spared
games.why: she vows to help beings in the lowest realms through lifetimes to come, and the sutra says she became Ksitigarbha.

practice: Bring to mind someone in a low place right now, a friend gone quiet, a relative in a hard season, a stranger who looks worn through.
Don't rush to fix anything; just stand beside them in your mind for a few breaths, the way Jizo stands at the roadside, not above them, not ahead of them, beside.
Then let one plain thing that might help come to mind: a message, a meal, an hour.

wordCard.voice: Ksitigarbha. The earth store: the bodhisattva who vows to help beings in the lowest realms, called Dizang in China and Jizo in Japan. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit: the name of the bodhisattva of the lowest realms, called Dizang in China and Jizo in Japan.
